content: Micronutrient deficiencies are prevalent among children with HIV, particularly in impoverished communities, and these deficiencies exacerbate the effects of HIV. Micronutrient supplementation has been proposed as a potentially effective and safe intervention to reduce the burden of HIV-related disease in children. This updated review builds on a prior Cochrane review, which found that vitamin A and zinc supplementation were both beneficial and safe for children exposed to or living with HIV. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of micronutrient supplementation in reducing mortality and morbidity among children with HIV. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were identified through searches of CENTRAL, EMBASE, and PubMed, using the Cochrane HIV/AIDS Group's search strategies. Eligible trials compared micronutrient supplements (including vitamins, trace elements, or combinations) to placebo, no treatment, or other supplements, with primary outcomes being mortality, morbidity, and HIV-related hospitalizations. Secondary outcomes included markers of HIV disease progression, anthropometric measures, and adverse effects of supplementation. Two independent reviewers screened and selected studies, assessed the risk of bias using standardized criteria, and extracted data. Statistical analyses were conducted using Review Manager 5.1, calculating risk ratios (RR) for dichotomous outcomes and weighted mean differences (WMD) for continuous outcomes, with random-effects meta-analyses performed when appropriate. The review included 11 studies with a total of 2,412 participants, adding three new studies to the eight included in the earlier review. These trials examined the effects of vitamin A (five trials), vitamin D (one trial), zinc (two trials), and multiple micronutrient supplements (three trials). All but one trial were conducted in African children. Vitamin A supplementation was shown to reduce all-cause mortality by 50% in a meta-analysis of three trials conducted in African children. However, its effects on diarrheal and respiratory morbidity were inconsistent. In one Tanzanian trial, vitamin A supplementation improved short-term growth. No significant adverse effects were reported in any of the trials involving vitamin A. A single small trial of vitamin D supplementation in North American children and adolescents demonstrated that it was safe but did not provide any clinical benefits. Zinc supplementation was found to reduce diarrheal morbidity without causing adverse effects on HIV disease progression in one small South African trial. Another South African trial, which included children with and without HIV, did not demonstrate any benefit from prophylactic zinc or multiple micronutrient supplementation compared to vitamin A in the subgroup of children with HIV. Multiple micronutrient supplementation at twice the recommended dietary allowance (RDA) did not significantly affect mortality, growth, or CD4 counts at 12 months in Ugandan children aged one to five years. However, short-term supplementation until hospital discharge reduced the duration of hospital admissions in poorly nourished South African children. Additionally, supplementation for six months post-discharge improved appetite and nutritional indicators. In conclusion, vitamin A supplementation is both beneficial and safe for children with HIV. Zinc supplementation is also safe and appears to reduce diarrheal morbidity in children with HIV, similar to its effects in children without HIV. Multiple micronutrient supplements may provide some clinical benefits in poorly nourished children with HIV, but their long-term effects, optimal composition, and dosing require further investigation. Additional trials are needed to evaluate the effects of single supplements, such as vitamin D, zinc, and selenium, and to better understand the role of multiple micronutrient supplementation in children with varying HIV disease statuses.
